plan.topic: Keeping results after stopping tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound): what the long-term evidence shows about keeping weight off. Regain varies a lot between people. The evidence links ongoing care and structured habits to holding on. Obesity is treated as a chronic condition.
plan.angle: Drop the ObesityWeek hook. Open with: 'Stopped tirzepatide, or thinking about life after it? Here's what the research shows about keeping results.' By 15 s: on average weight tends to come back after stopping, but how much varies widely, and ongoing care and habits are linked to keeping more of it off. Use the Cleveland Clinic cohort only if the peer-reviewed paper or abstract loads, and then only as one line: 'In one real-world observational study of semaglutide or tirzepatide, people who stopped after 3 to 12 months had lost less to begin with, and 45% of the obesity group held their weight or kept losing over a year. It's observational and covers both drugs.' Otherwise leave it out. Keep all SURMOUNT-4, BMJ and SURMOUNT-1 figures at their exact scope. Retitle to 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Keeping Weight Off After' (49 characters) or 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Can You Keep the Results?' (49 characters). Keep the thumbnail 'KEEP IT OFF?' as planned.
plan.target_keyword: how to keep weight off after mounjaro
plan.why: It's priority action #2 and on the double-down list. Stopping is our best recent broad video (6.35% CTR, 309 min by day 10), and ObesityWeek coverage is pushing the same search right now. | fact-check: This is a broad, searched question and the core evidence holds up: SURMOUNT-4 (335 vs 335, +14.0% regain on placebo from week 36 to 88, placebo still 9.9% below baseline), the BMJ 2025 regain meta-analysis, the SURMOUNT-1 off-treatment period in adults with prediabetes, and guidelines that call obesity a chronic disease. Two things need changing. (1) The ObesityWeek hook dates an evergreen video, which breaks the craft rule against 'now', 'new' and conference-dated framing. It also points to the Cleveland Clinic cohort, which I could only trace to newsroom and secondary coverage. That cohort is observational, real-world and covers semaglutide AND tirzepatide. People stopped after 3–12 months having lost only about 8.4% on average, and 27% switched to another medicine within the year. So its '45% held or kept losing' figure (obesity group only) can't be set beside trial figures or credited to tirzepatide alone. (2) 'How to Keep Results' promises a proven method, but the habit evidence only supports 'linked to'. Everything else in the angle (habit hedging, kidney caveat, no stopping, tapering or dosing advice, the case reports left out) is sound.

package.pinned_comment: In SURMOUNT-4, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, were switched to placebo after 36 weeks on tirzepatide. Their weight went up 14%, on average, over the next year. They still finished 9.9% below where they started. And about 1 in 6 of them kept at least 80% of the weight they lost in the first 36 weeks. Save this for your next appointment. Please don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Make that decision with your prescriber. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, fifty-one. A year on tirzepatide, and the ten p.m. food noise she used to fight has gone quiet.
She and her prescriber are talking about what comes next. And there's one worry she can't shake: if the medicine stops, does it all come back?
If you've felt that worry, or felt guilty about it, you're not alone. And the biology says it isn't only a willpower problem.
So what actually happens when researchers swap the medicine for a dummy, without telling anyone?
scenes.on_screen_text: What if you swap it secretly?

scenes.narration: That's exactly what SURMOUNT-4 did, with tirzepatide, the medicine in Mounjaro and Zepbound.
Everyone took tirzepatide for thirty-six weeks first, at the highest dose they could tolerate, with lifestyle counselling.
In that time, they lost about a fifth of their body weight, on average. Twenty point nine percent.
scenes.on_screen_text: About a fifth of body weight

scenes.narration: Then came the twist. Six hundred seventy people were randomly split. Three hundred thirty-five kept taking tirzepatide, and three hundred thirty-five were switched to placebo.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide vs placebo, randomized at week 36

scenes.narration: Neither the participants nor their doctors knew who got which. And both groups kept getting the same lifestyle counselling.
So the big difference between the groups over the next year was whether the medicine was still there.
By week eighty-eight, the group that stayed on tirzepatide had kept losing. Five point five percent more, on average.
The placebo group went the other way. Their weight rose fourteen percent, on average, over the same year.
Over the whole trial, from the start to week eighty-eight: tirzepatide, down twenty-five point three percent. Placebo, down nine point nine percent.
So two things are true at once. Stopping led to substantial regain, on average. And a year later, the placebo group hadn't gone all the way back.

visual.myth: Stopping means back to square one
visual.fact: SURMOUNT-4 placebo group: big regain on average, still 9.9% below start at week 88

scenes.narration: Back to Dana. If she stopped, that's the average picture. But Dana isn't an average. Hold that thought.
scenes.retention_device: Return to thread; opens a mini-loop

scenes.narration: First, the question everyone asks. Why does the weight come back at all?
Here's the part that might take some guilt off your shoulders.

visual.stock_query: backpack of guilt being set down

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide acts on two hormone receptors, GIP and GLP-1. Those signals are involved in appetite and how much we eat.
The label puts its half-life at about five days. So after a last dose, levels of the medicine fall away over the following weeks.
But here's where it gets weird. Your body has its own defence system for weight.

In a small Australian study, fifty adults with overweight or obesity, without diabetes, started a very low-calorie diet. Researchers then tracked the hormones of those who stayed in the study for about a year.
scenes.on_screen_text: Small diet study, one year tracked

scenes.narration: A year later, hunger-related hormones were still shifted toward eating more. And on average, people rated their appetite higher than before they lost the weight.
That study was about dieting, not tirzepatide. But it shows how hard the body can push back after weight loss.
Canada's adult obesity guideline describes obesity as a complex, progressive and relapsing chronic disease.
Think of how we treat high blood pressure: as something you manage over time, not a one-off fix. That guideline frames obesity care the same way, as long-term care.
So if weight starts creeping back for you, it isn't proof you did something wrong. Your biology is pushing back.
But the scale isn't the only thing that changes when the medicine stops. And the next finding surprised me.

visual.stock_query: scale with heart and lab tube

scenes.narration: What else changes when the medicine stops?
SURMOUNT-1 followed adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, who also had prediabetes. They took tirzepatide or placebo for 176 weeks, a little over three years.
By the end of treatment, one point three percent of the tirzepatide group had developed type 2 diabetes. On placebo, it was thirteen point three percent.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide vs placebo, type 2 diabetes, week 176

scenes.narration: Then everyone stopped for seventeen weeks. By the end of that break, the tirzepatide group's figure had risen to two point four percent. Placebo's was thirteen point seven percent.
So diabetes cases ticked up once treatment stopped. But after those seventeen weeks, the tirzepatide group was still well below placebo.

visual.stock_query: small step up on low staircase

scenes.narration: It's one trial, in people with prediabetes, over a short break. But it's a reminder that results are about health, not just a number on the scale.

visual.stock_query: heart and scale side by side

scenes.narration: Those are single trials. So what happens when you pool everything?
Let's zoom out.
A systematic review in The BMJ pooled thirty-seven studies of people who stopped weight-management medicines, all types combined.

visual.stat_label: Studies pooled, weight-management medicines, all types

scenes.narration: On average, weight came back at about zero point four kilograms a month after stopping. That's just under a pound.

visual.stat_label: Average regain after stopping, all medicines pooled
visual.stock_query: one small apple on a scale

scenes.narration: At that pace, the authors projected weight would return to its starting point about one point seven years after stopping. That's a projection, on average, across all those medicines.

visual.stat_label: Projected return to baseline, pooled average

scenes.narration: For the newer medicines, semaglutide and tirzepatide, the review found regain was faster. About zero point eight kilograms a month, with a projected return to the starting point at about one point five years. These medicines also tend to lead to more weight loss in the first place.
scenes.on_screen_text: Newer medicines: about 0.8 kg a month

visual.stat_label: BMJ review, semaglutide and tirzepatide studies, average regain after stopping

scenes.retention_device: Twist: the figure that matters for this drug

scenes.narration: In the studies it compared, regain was faster after stopping medicines than after ending behavioural weight programmes, by about zero point three kilograms a month.

And STEP 1, a trial of semaglutide, a different GLP-1 medicine, followed adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, for a year after stopping. On average, they regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost.

visual.stat_label: STEP 1 extension, semaglutide, one year off

scenes.narration: Different drug, different trial, so don't compare those numbers directly. But the direction is consistent.
So is there anything that tips the odds? This is where it gets more hopeful.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: Here's the honest version. There's no proven formula. But there are clear patterns.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: The first is ongoing treatment itself. In SURMOUNT-4, continuing tirzepatide kept and added to the weight loss, while switching to placebo led to substantial regain.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: Whether long-term treatment fits your life is a decision for you and your prescriber, together. Not a rule from a video.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: The second pattern is habits. The National Weight Control Registry studies thousands of people who lost at least thirty pounds and kept it off for at least a year.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: They tend to report the same few things: a lot of physical activity, a consistent eating pattern, eating breakfast, and checking their weight regularly.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: And one more: catching small slips early, before they turn into bigger regains.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: Big caveat: that registry is self-selected and observational, and it started long before these medicines. So these habits are linked to keeping weight off, not proven to cause it.

visual.myth: These habits guarantee you keep it off
visual.fact: Observational registry: habits are linked to maintenance, not proven to cause it

scenes.narration: Picture Dana with a plan. Not a crash diet. A routine she can actually keep.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: That might mean protein at each meal and some strength training, to support her muscles.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor before raising your protein.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: Movement she enjoys, regular meals, and a simple way to notice drift early, like a weekly weigh-in, if that feels okay for her.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: The third pattern is easy to overlook: ongoing care. Keep seeing your care team, even when things feel stable. A dietitian or obesity specialist can help adjust the plan as life changes.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: And if side effects are part of why you're thinking about stopping, say so. The label says stomach side effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time, and your prescriber may have options.

scenes.section: What's linked to keeping it off
scenes.narration: Please don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Make that decision with your prescriber.
scenes.on_screen_text: Please don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Make that decision with your prescriber.

scenes.narration: Okay. The number I promised at the start.
Remember the three hundred thirty-five people switched to placebo in SURMOUNT-4?
Researchers checked how many kept at least eighty percent of the weight they had lost during the first thirty-six weeks.
On tirzepatide, eighty-nine point five percent did. On placebo, sixteen point six percent did.
Sixteen point six percent is about one in six. Picture six people switched to placebo. About one of them still held on to at least eighty percent of their loss a year later.

visual.stock_query: six friends at table, one highlighted

scenes.narration: Averages hide people. Some regained a lot, some less, and some held on.
The trial didn't test why those people did better, so I won't pretend to know. But it tells Dana something important: regain isn't a fixed destiny.
It's a range. And the evidence links ongoing treatment, care and habits to holding on to more.

scenes.narration: So here's what to bring to your next appointment.
One: ask what long-term care looks like for you, with or without medicine.
Two: work on habits you can keep for years. Protein, strength training, movement you enjoy, regular meals.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe. It can ship once the four small wording fixes below are applied.

**What I checked:**
- **SURMOUNT-4:** population, open-label 36-week lead-in at the highest tolerated dose, −20.9%, 670 randomized (335 vs 335), double-blind, −5.5% vs +14.0% from week 36 to 88, −25.3% vs −9.9% from week 0 to 88, and 89.5% vs 16.6% keeping at least 80% of their loss.
- **SURMOUNT-1 3-year (prediabetes):** 1.3% vs 13.3% at week 176, and 2.4% vs 13.7% at week 193 after 17 weeks off.
- **BMJ 2026 review (West et al., PMID 41500720):** 37 studies, 0.4 kg a month, about 1.7 years, 0.8 kg a month and about 1.5 years for semaglutide and tirzepatide, and 0.3 kg a month faster than behavioural programmes. That last figure holds regardless of initial weight loss.
- **The rest:** the two-thirds regain in the STEP 1 extension, the Sumithran 2011 design (50 adults, very-low-calorie diet, about a year of follow-up), the CMAJ 2020 wording ("complex, progressive and relapsing chronic disease"), the NWCR habits including catching slips early, and the label's roughly 5-day half-life and dual GIP/GLP-1 action.

**Framing and safety:**
- Diet-study vs tirzepatide, observational vs causal, and different-trial vs head-to-head are all hedged correctly.
- Each trial keeps its exact population.
- The kidney-disease caveat, the "if that feels okay" note on self-weighing, the don't-stop line, "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line are all there.
- Dana is clearly hypothetical, and the title's promise is paid off.

**Source access:**
- PubMed pages wouldn't load (cookie wall). I confirmed the PMIDs and numbers through search results and the publishers' or universities' own pages.
- The Lilly PDF exists but its text couldn't be parsed. The half-life and GI-timing wording match our established label facts, but I couldn't re-check them in the text myself.

issues.claim: Ongoing treatment, care and habits are linked to keeping more of it off (tagged surmount4, bmj2026, nwcr)
issues.problem: The 'care' part isn't in any of the tagged sources. The NWCR covers habits and SURMOUNT-4 covers treatment. Long-term care comes from the CMAJ guideline.
issues.fix: Add 'cmaj2020' to source_ids in s02 and s72. Drop 'bmj2026' from s02: the review shows regain, not what helps people keep weight off.

issues.claim: For the newer medicines, semaglutide and tirzepatide, the review found regain was faster. About zero point eight kilograms a month…
issues.problem: A viewer could read 'faster' as these drugs being worse once stopped. The context is that they also produce more weight loss to start with. The review's 0.3 kg a month comparison with behavioural programmes is adjusted for initial loss, but this 0.8 figure isn't.
issues.fix: Narration: "For the newer medicines, semaglutide and tirzepatide, the review found regain was faster. About zero point eight kilograms a month, with a projected return to the starting point at about one point five years. These medicines also tend to lead to more weight loss in the first place." On-screen text stays the same.

issues.claim: It's biology doing what biology does.
issues.problem: This overstates the case. The evidence shows that biology pushes back strongly, not that regain is purely biological. s10 hedges it correctly ('isn't only a willpower problem').
issues.fix: Narration: "So if weight starts creeping back for you, it isn't proof you did something wrong. Your biology is pushing back."

issues.claim: Regain is biology, not a verdict on you.
issues.problem: Same overstatement as s33, in the recap.
issues.fix: Narration: "And five: be kind to yourself. Regain has real biology behind it. It's not a verdict on you."

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean, single-focal-point layouts with legible bold text at phone size (no cut-off, no overlap). However, the title is "Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Can You Keep the Results?" — candidate #0's "KEEP IT OFF?" and candidate #2's "WHO KEEPS IT?" both reuse the title's own key word ("Keep"/"Keeps"), triggering the hard cap that text repeating the title's words caps ctr at 5. Candidate #1, "14%" + "BACK IN A YEAR?", introduces a fresh, concrete, credible stake (SURMOUNT-4's 14.0% regain figure) that doesn't restate the title, keeps the gap open (viewer still needs the video to learn if/why/how to avoid it), and pairs with a shocked-mascot expression that matches the alarming stat — satisfying the emotion-match rule. Legibility is strong across all three; #1's two-tier text (giant "14%" plus a readable sub-label) remains clear even at 168px. Since #0 and #2 are capped by the repeated-title-word rule, #1 is the best pick on CTR potential while maintaining legibility ≥7 and no misleading content.

issues.claim: In SURMOUNT-4, adults switched to placebo after 36 weeks on tirzepatide saw their weight go up 14%... And about 1 in 6 kept at least 80% of their loss.
issues.problem: The comment cuts the trial population down to "adults". The script and the description both give the full SURMOUNT-4 population. The 1-in-6 line also leaves out that it refers to the weight lost in the first 36 weeks, measured a year after the switch. The script says both.
issues.fix: In SURMOUNT-4, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, were switched to placebo after 36 weeks on tirzepatide. Their weight went up 14%, on average, over the next year. They still finished 9.9% below where they started. And about 1 in 6 of them kept at least 80% of the weight they lost in the first 36 weeks. Save this for your next appointment. Please don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Make that decision with your prescriber. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
